title: 30 Years of COBOL and Banking Systems: What Do You Know That Modern Developers Have Forgotten?
summary:
Have you spent decades working with COBOL in financial systems? Then you probably know things that many modern developers don't even realize they need to know.

I want to interview you!

I've opened a GitHub discussion with 18 questions for professionals who have worked with COBOL, mainframes, and banking systems. I want to hear your stories about production failures, batch processing, business rules hidden deep in the code, and the decisions that kept financial systems running for decades.

You don't need to answer all 18 questions. Pick just one, share a story, or tell us something you learned along the way. Even a small piece of your experience could help preserve knowledge that future generations of developers might otherwise lose.

This initiative is part of FinKore, an open-source project focused on documenting and preserving fundamental financial rules for future generations of developers.

I don't want to know whether COBOL is better than Java. I want to discover what you've learned over 30 years that we're still trying to reinvent today.

Would you be willing to share your experience in this open interview?

title: I turned my AI coding agents into an "office" so anyone can run them
summary:
I'm the maker of AI Office, a free and open source (MIT) desktop app for macOS (Apple Silicon) and Windows.

Why I built it

AI coding agents like Claude Code are powerful, but they live in terminal windows. If you are not a developer, a terminal is a wall. Even if you are one, running several agents at once gets messy: which window is working, which one is waiting for my OK, and what did it actually change?

So I moved the whole thing into an office.

  • AI agents are staff. You hire Claude or GPT staff, give them work in plain chat, and they report back when they're done.
  • You can see them work. Each agent sits at a desk in an office view. At a glance you see who is working, who is resting, and who is waiting for you.
  • Risky stuff needs your approval. File changes and shell commands land in an approval inbox first. Nothing risky runs until you say yes, and you can undo a change.
  • Big jobs go to a team lead. The lead plans the work, splits it up, and asks you to confirm before anything starts.

You don't need to know commands. "Hire staff, give work, approve" is enough. (Your company also levels up as staff work, and the office grows. A small thing, but it makes it fun.)

What you need

Claude Code or ChatGPT (Codex) already signed in on your computer. No API key. Usage is billed to that account, so running many staff at once uses your limits faster.

Everything stays on your computer. There are no analytics. The only network calls are update checks and downloads.

Not great yet

  • Not code-signed, so macOS shows an "unidentified developer" warning the first time (System Settings > Privacy & Security > Open Anyway).
  • Apple Silicon only on Mac, no Intel Mac or Linux.
  • On Windows, notifications from outside staff, question handling, and screen capture are missing.

Try it / feedback

  • Site and demo: https://engchoon.github.io/ai-office/
  • Source: https://github.com/EngChooN/ai-office

I would love to hear where setup got stuck, and where the approval flow felt annoying. Especially if you are not a developer: was the "office" idea easier to understand than a terminal?

title: DesignSystemKit: one design system for SwiftUI and UIKit, with runtime white-label theming
summary:
If you've built white-label apps, tenant-branded apps or even just a SwiftUI rewrite of a UIKit app, you know the pain: colours hard-coded in three places, buttons that look slightly different on every screen, and a dark mode that only half works.

DesignSystemKit is my answer: a native design system for SwiftUI and UIKit, distributed with Swift Package Manager. One set of tokens, typography, components and icons, with themes you can switch at runtime for white-label apps, tenant branding and seasonal skins. Free, MIT licensed, and no third-party dependencies.

What's inside

Module What it gives you
DesignSystemCore Semantic colour tokens (light + dark), spacing, radius, border, elevation and motion scales, typography, DSTheme, ThemeStore with persistence, a tenant ThemeRegistry, a ThemeValidator that checks WCAG contrast, and field validation. No UI framework imports.
DesignSystemAssets Bundled Poppins fonts, a semantic icon catalog with SF Symbol fallback, and localized component strings (English, Spanish, German, Arabic, Hindi) with plurals.
DesignSystemSwiftUI .appTheme(...), @ThemeTokens, Dynamic Type text styles and components including buttons, text fields, checkbox, radio, toggle, picker, date field, card, badge, chip, banner, progress, dialog, empty state, skeleton/shimmer and more.
DesignSystemUIKit Dynamic UIColors and Dynamic Type UIFonts, theme observation for view controllers, window appearance binding, DSUIButton, DSUITextField, DSUICardView, DSUIBadge, DSUILabel.
DesignSystemPreview A browsable catalog of every token and component with a live theme switcher.

Requirements: iOS 16+, iPadOS 16+, Mac Catalyst 16+, macOS 13+ (Core, Assets and SwiftUI). Xcode 16 or later, Swift 6 toolchain.

Install 

.package(url: "https://github.com/eeshuu/DesignSystemKit.git", from: "1.0.0"),
// …
.target(name: "App", dependencies: [
    .product(name: "DesignSystemSwiftUI", package: "DesignSystemKit"),
    .product(name: "DesignSystemUIKit", package: "DesignSystemKit"), // only if you use UIKit
]),

Fonts, icons and translations ship with the package. Nothing has to be copied into your app.

SwiftUI in a few lines 

@main
struct MyApp: App {
    @StateObject private var store = ThemeStore(persistence: UserDefaultsThemePersistence())
    init() { FontRegistry.registerBundledFonts() }

    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup { ContentView().appTheme(store: store) } // once, at the root
    }
}

struct ContentView: View {
    @ThemeTokens private var ds
    @State private var email = ""

    var body: some View {
        VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: ds.spacing.lg) {
            DSText("Welcome back", style: .title)
            DSTextField("Email", text: $email, kind: .email,
                        validation: FieldValidator([.email("Enter a valid email")], isOptional: true).validate(email),
                        isRequired: true)
            DSButton("Continue", trailingIcon: .arrowRight, fullWidth: true) { }
        }
        .padding(ds.spacing.xl)
        .background(ds.colors.background)
    }
}

UIKit gets the same tokens 

final class ProfileViewController: UIViewController, DSThemeable {
    private let store: ThemeStore
    private var subscription: DSThemeSubscription?
    private let titleLabel = DSUILabel(style: .heading1, text: "Profile")
    private let save = DSUIButton(title: "Save", variant: .primary)

    override func viewDidLoad() {
        super.viewDidLoad()
        subscription = store.observe(self) // applies now and on every theme change
    }

    func apply(theme: DSTheme) {
        view.backgroundColor = .ds(.background, theme: theme)
        titleLabel.apply(theme: theme)
        save.apply(theme: theme)
    }
}

Mixed apps work in both directions: DSHostingController themes SwiftUI inside UIKit, and the store is available via @Environment(\.dsThemeStore) for UIKit inside SwiftUI.

Runtime theming and white-label 

store.selectTheme(id: "forest")         // brand theme
store.setAppearance(.dark)              // .system, .light or .dark
store.selectTheme(forTenant: "acme")    // tenant mapping you registered

Four themes are built in (standard, forest, sunset and midnight). Create your own in code, or load one from JSON; anything the file leaves out falls back to the standard theme:

var brand = DSTheme.standard
brand.id = "acme"
brand.light[.primary] = "#D9480F"
brand.dark[.primary] = "#FFA94D"
brand.components.buttonShape = .pill
store.apply(brand) // validated, including WCAG contrast; refused if it has errors

{ "id": "acme", "name": "Acme", "light": { "primary": "#D9480F" }, "components": { "buttonShape": "pill" } }

That means a server can ship a tenant's branding as a small JSON file, and a bad palette with unreadable contrast gets rejected instead of shipped.

Accessibility and quality

The test suites cover token values, contrast of every built-in palette, theme JSON, persistence, font registration, localization and plurals, Dynamic Type scaling, UIKit observation, and snapshots in light and dark. The sample app's UI tests cover theme switching, tenants, form validation, accessibility identifiers, mixed navigation and the largest Dynamic Type size.

The repo includes a sample app (Examples/DesignSystemDemo) with a component catalog, a SwiftUI sign-up screen, a UIKit profile screen and a settings tab for theme, appearance and tenant switching.

My other Swift packages

  • SecureStorageKit: Keychain, Face ID and Secure Enclave storage
  • AppLoggerKit: privacy-first logging with OSLog, JSON Lines, redaction and export

github.com/eeshuu/DesignSystemKit: MIT licensed (bundled Poppins fonts under the SIL Open Font License). Stars, issues and feedback are very welcome.

title: AppLoggerKit: privacy-first logging for Swift apps (OSLog, JSON Lines, redaction, export)
summary:
Logs are one of the most common places sensitive data leaks from an iOS app. They end up in sysdiagnoses, support emails, crash tickets and bug trackers, and a single print("\(user)") or "token=\(token)" can put an email address or a bearer token in all of them.

I wanted Apple's unified logging, optional log files users can send to support, and real privacy guarantees, without pulling in a third-party SDK. So I built AppLoggerKit: a free, MIT-licensed logging and local diagnostics package for Swift, SwiftUI and UIKit with no third-party dependencies.

What's inside

Module What it gives you
AppLoggerCore AppLogger with seven levels, lazy messages, categories and scoped loggers; structured LogRecord with a versioned JSON schema; public / private / sensitive metadata; a Redactor; LogContext for correlation IDs. Foundation only.
AppLoggerOSLog os.Logger output with level mapping, Console.app filtering and OSLog privacy annotations.
AppLoggerFile JSON Lines files with size/time rotation and retention, streaming search, paging, statistics, and redacted JSON Lines / text / ZIP exports.
AppLoggerUI Optional SwiftUI and UIKit log viewer, live console, ShareLink export button and \.appLogger in the environment.
AppLoggerTesting In-memory and failing destinations plus AppLogger.capturing() for your tests.

Requirements: iOS 16+, iPadOS 16+, Mac Catalyst 16+, macOS 13+. Xcode 16 or later, Swift 6 toolchain.

Install 

.package(url: "https://github.com/eeshuu/AppLoggerKit.git", from: "1.0.0"),
// …
.target(name: "App", dependencies: [
    .product(name: "AppLoggerCore", package: "AppLoggerKit"),
    .product(name: "AppLoggerOSLog", package: "AppLoggerKit"),
    .product(name: "AppLoggerFile", package: "AppLoggerKit"), // only if you want log files
]),

Quick start 

import AppLoggerCore
import AppLoggerFile
import AppLoggerOSLog

let fileLog = FileLogDestination(configuration: .default) // opt-in: no files without it

let logger = AppLogger(configuration: .init(
    subsystem: "com.example.myapp",
    minimumLevel: .debug,
    categoryLevels: ["network": .trace],
    destinations: [OSLogDestination(), fileLog]
))

logger.info("Application launched", category: "lifecycle")
logger.error("Unable to load profile", metadata: ["feature": "profile", "attempt": 2], error: error)

Messages and metadata are autoclosures, so a call below the active level never builds its string.

Privacy is the main feature

Nothing is captured automatically. No request or response bodies, headers, device identifiers or user data. Only what you pass is logged.

Metadata has a privacy class, enforced by the compiler. Literals are public; runtime values must say what they are, so "\(user.email)" doesn't compile as metadata:

logger.notice("Signed in", metadata: [
    "method": "password",              // public literal
    "userID": .private(user.id),       // shown in live outputs, redacted from files and exports
    "token": .sensitive(token),        // never reaches any destination
    "endpoint": .url(request.url!),    // credentials, fragment and query values stripped
])

Redaction runs before every destination. Keys like authorization, token, password, secret, cookie and api_key are redacted whatever their class, and bearer tokens, JWTs and password=… patterns are scrubbed from messages, values and error descriptions. You can add your own rules.

Files and exports are stricter. Private values are redacted by default, and an export re-applies redaction to whatever was stored.

Correlation IDs that follow async code 

try await LogContext.withCorrelationID(requestID) {
    logger.info("Fetching profile")
    try await api.loadProfile() // every log inside, at any depth, carries the ID
}

Search and export logs on device

Perfect for a "Send logs to support" button:

let reader = LogReader(store: fileLog.store)
let recentErrors = try await reader.tail(matching: LogQuery(minimumLevel: .error, since: .now - 3600))

await logger.flush()
let export = try await LogExporter(store: fileLog.store).export(LogExportRequest(
    format: .zip,              // logs.jsonl + logs.txt + manifest.json
    query: LogQuery(since: .now - 86_400),
    maxBytes: 5_000_000,
    note: "Ticket 4821"
))
// Present export.url with ShareLink or UIActivityViewController(logExport: export).

Built for Swift 6 concurrency

Every API is safe from any thread or actor. Log calls never block on I/O: records are queued under a lock and delivered in order by one background task. OSLogDestination writes on the calling thread so the last records before a crash aren't lost. Levels can be changed at runtime from a debug menu or remote flag without touching call sites, and a destination that throws never affects the call site.

Testable 

import AppLoggerTesting

@Test func loadingLogsProgress() async {
    let (logger, capture) = AppLogger.capturing()
    await ProfileRepository(logger: logger).load()
    await logger.flush()
    #expect(capture.messages == ["Loading profile", "Profile loaded"])
}

What it deliberately doesn't do

No hosted dashboards or remote ingestion, no analytics or behaviour tracking, no crash reporting, and no encrypted storage: log files are ordinary local files protected by iOS file protection and excluded from backups. If you need to store secrets, that's what my other package, SecureStorageKit, is for.

The repo includes a sample app (Examples/LoggerDemo) and docs on architecture, privacy and the file format.

title: I built bhasha-kit: a free offline Python library for Hindi & Bengali text
summary:
Hi everyone! I'm Solo Developer. I just published my first Python package, bhasha-kit, a free, offline toolkit for Hindi, Bengali and English text.

Why I built it

Most text tools need an API key or an internet connection, and many don't handle Hindi and Bengali well. I wanted something simple that runs locally, with no dependencies.

What it does

  • Cleans text (emojis, extra spaces, Unicode)

title: Try a self-hosted Google Business Profile manager before Google approves your API access
summary:
If you manage Google Business Profiles for clients, the slowest step in trying any API-based tool is usually Google itself: you request Business Profile API access for your own Google Cloud project, and approval can take a few days. OpenGMB, the open-source GBP manager we build, has a mock mode for exactly that gap. This post is the short version of how to run it locally and click through everything with sample data first.

Disclosure: we build OpenGMB. The community edition is MIT licensed.

What you need

  • Docker Engine 24 or newer with the Compose plugin
  • About 4 GB of free RAM while the images build
  • A public HTTPS hostname, only if you want Google sign-in
  • An authenticator app, because two-factor sign-in is required

Run it 

git clone https://github.com/synectus/OpenGMB.git
cd OpenGMB/deploy/selfhost
cp .env.example .env     # set OWNER_EMAIL and OWNER_PASSWORD
docker compose up -d --build

The comments in .env.example explain every value. Then open http://localhost:8080, sign in with the owner email and password, enrol your authenticator app and keep the backup codes it shows.

Use the sample Google account

The Google client starts in mock mode. Under Settings → Google, press "Use the sample Google account" to import sample locations. From there you can look at the parts that matter before you connect a real profile:

  • Reviews: one inbox for every location's Google reviews. Assign them, add internal notes, and draft replies yourself, with templates or with AI.
  • Posts: write, schedule and approve posts for one location or many, with a calendar of what is scheduled or published.
  • Profile health: a health score with the checks behind it, and edits to hours, categories and services across many locations in one change.
  • Performance: calls, website clicks, direction requests and impressions per location.

AI drafts use your own Anthropic key (no credits, no markup), and rank tracking uses your own DataForSEO account. In mock mode you can leave both out.

What to test while you are in there: the approval rules

The part worth testing with sample data is what happens before anything would reach Google. In the community edition:

  • Posts and profile edits always need a person's approval.
  • Replies to 1 to 3 star reviews always need a person and are never published automatically.
  • Replies to 4 and 5 star reviews need a person, unless the owner turns on auto-approve for that client.
  • Every reply, post and edit is checked by guardrail rules first: links, emails, phone numbers, offers, bad hours, banned words. Blocks cannot be overridden; warnings must be acknowledged.

Healthcare and law firm clients get extra rule packs, and the rules run again just before anything is sent to Google.

When you are ready to go live

Request Business Profile API access for your own Google Cloud project and wait for Google's approval. The full guide covers ports, email, Google, backups and upgrades: OpenGMB self-hosting guide.

The code is synectus/OpenGMB on GitHub.

title: SecureStorageKit: a dependency-free Swift package for Keychain, Face ID and Secure Enclave storage
summary:
Every iOS app I've worked on in the last decade ended up with its own hand-rolled Keychain wrapper. Most of them had the same bugs: errSecDuplicateItem not handled, queries that didn't match the attributes used to save, background reads failing with errSecInteractionNotAllowed and logging the user out, and tokens quietly ending up in print statements.

So I packaged the patterns I keep rewriting into SecureStorageKit: a free, open-source Swift package for storing secrets on iOS, iPadOS and macOS. It's serverless, built only on Apple frameworks (Keychain, LocalAuthentication, CryptoKit and the Secure Enclave), and has no third-party dependencies.

What's inside

Area Features
Keychain Save, read, update and delete Strings, Data and Codable values. Scoped clear, accessibility options, access groups, iCloud sync, typed errors, migration from legacy Keychain wrappers.
Biometrics Item-level Face ID / Touch ID / passcode protection, biometryCurrentSet, availability checks and lockout.
Crypto AES-256-GCM in a versioned envelope, HKDF, key manager (create, rotate, retire), recoverable key rotation engine, streaming encrypted file vault, Secure Enclave signing and sealing.
Accounts Token store with refresh, per-account isolation and logout cleanup; multi-account vault.
Ops Redacted logging, audit log, in-memory mock, versioned Codable migrations, password-protected backup and restore.

Requirements: iOS 15+, macOS 12+, Mac Catalyst 15+, Swift 6 toolchain (Xcode 16 or later).

Install

In Xcode: File ▸ Add Package Dependencies… and paste the repo URL. Or in Package.swift:

.package(url: "https://github.com/eeshuu/SecureStorageKit.git", from: "1.0.1"),
// …
.target(name: "App", dependencies: [
    .product(name: "SecureStorageKit", package: "SecureStorageKit"),
]),

Quick start 

import SecureStorageKit

let storage = SecureStorage(service: "my-app")

try await storage.save("secret", forKey: "access_token")
let token: String? = try await storage.retrieve("access_token", as: String.self)
try await storage.delete("access_token")
try await storage.clearAll() // only this namespace, nothing else

// Protected by the Keychain item itself: no Face ID, no data.
try await storage.save("private", forKey: "vault", protection: .biometryCurrentSet)
let value: String? = try await storage.retrieve("vault", as: String.self,
                                                authenticationReason: "Unlock secure data")

retrieve returns nil when the key doesn't exist, and every failure is a typed StorageError.

A few things I'm proud of

Tokens that refresh themselves, once. Concurrent callers share a single refresh, and token values print as .

let tokens = SecureTokenStore(service: "my-app", refresher: AuthAPI())
let bearer = try await tokens.validAccessToken(for: "alice") // refreshes once, even if called concurrently
try await tokens.logout(account: "alice") // tokens + session secrets

Encryption with real key rotation. Old data keeps decrypting while new data uses the new key; retire the old one when nothing needs it.

let keys = KeyManager(storage: SecureStorage(service: "my-app", namespace: "keys"))
let sealed = try await keys.encrypt(data, associatedData: Data(recordID.utf8))
try await keys.rotate()            // new data uses default#2; default#1 still decrypts
try await keys.retire(version: 1)  // destroys default#1 once nothing uses it

Secure Enclave keys that never leave the chip.

let se = SecureEnclaveManager(storage: storage.namespaced("se"))
let publicKey = try await se.createSigningKey(tag: "device", protection: .biometryCurrentSet)
let signature = try await se.sign(challenge, tag: "device", prompt: .init(reason: "Approve sign-in"))

Testable without a device. An in-memory Keychain lets you simulate Face ID cancel, a new fingerprint, or a locked device in unit tests.

let mock = InMemoryKeychain()
let storage = SecureStorage(configuration: .init(service: "test"), backend: mock)
mock.authenticationResult = .failure(.userCancelled)
mock.simulateBiometryEnrollmentChange()
mock.isDeviceLocked = true

Easy migration. Import existing items from KeychainAccess, SwiftKeychainWrapper or raw SecItem code with MigrationManager.

The repo also ships a SwiftUI demo app (Keychain, Biometrics, Encryption and Tokens tabs), 66 unit tests, a full API reference and a written threat model.

An honest note

SecureStorageKit has a full test suite but has not had an independent security audit yet. The threat model in Docs/ThreatModel.md spells out what is and isn't protected. If you work in security, reviews, issues and PRs are very welcome.

Want the background?

If you'd like the reasoning behind these choices (accessibility classes, ThisDeviceOnly, biometry binding, Secure Enclave keys), I wrote a long guide: iOS Application Security: SSL Pinning, Keychain, API Encryption and App Attest.

github.com/eeshuu/SecureStorageKit: a star helps other iOS devs find it. MIT licensed.

My other Swift packages

  • AppLoggerKit: privacy-first logging with OSLog, JSON Lines, redaction and export
  • DesignSystemKit: one design system for SwiftUI and UIKit, with runtime white-label theming

title: I review my AI agent's code like a merge request
summary:
These days most of the code in my side projects is written by Claude Code. I describe what I want, it writes, I review. My job moved from writing code to reviewing it.

And reviewing in a terminal is bad. You get a wall of diff, scroll up, scroll down, and then type something like "in server.ts, around line 40, the host should be configurable" into the chat. It works, but it's nothing like a real code review. So I built a small tool for it. It's called Feedbacker, and it gives the agent a merge request page it can open for me.

In this post, I'll walk you through:

  • what Feedbacker does
  • how the agent asks for a review
  • what I changed after the first real reviews
  • the decisions and gotchas along the way

The itch

A few years ago I wrote about how to be good at code reviews. Most of it still holds when the author is an AI. What doesn't hold is the tooling. GitHub and GitLab are great for reviewing, but I don't want to push every half-done change to a branch and open an MR just to tell the agent it named something wrong.

Two more things made it worse for me:

  • Several repos at once. One task often touches more than one repo, and I want to see the whole change together.
  • Git worktrees. I sometimes run more than one agent in parallel, each in its own worktree. Reviewing that in a terminal is no fun at all.

What I wanted: the agent finishes, opens a page in my browser with the diffs of everything it changed, I comment on lines like in an MR, click a button, and my comments go back to the agent.

What it does

  • All repos on one page. The agent passes a list of repo paths, anywhere on disk, each with its own base. With --worktrees it pulls in every worktree of a repo, labelled with its branch.
  • Line comments. Click a line number to comment, shift-click to cover a range. A comment is either Comment (change something) or Ask (a question the agent has to answer).
  • Approve or Request changes. That sends everything back to the agent and closes the page.
  • Where to look. The agent writes a short summary and points me to the places it thinks matter most.
  • Sorted by kind. Code first, then tests, config, docs and generated files (lock files, build output). Only code starts expanded.
  • Local only. It runs on 127.0.0.1 with a random token in the URL, only reads git, and nothing leaves my machine.

How the agent asks

The easiest way is the Claude Code plugin:

claude plugin marketplace add PavlikPolivka/feedbacker
claude plugin install feedbacker@feedbacker

Then I just say "let me review it". The plugin gives Claude an MCP tool, request_review, and a skill that tells it when to use it. The tool call blocks until I submit, and the result is markdown the agent can act on:

# Review feedback

Verdict: **changes requested**

## Comments

### /home/me/Projects/api

**src/server.ts:6** (new side)

```diff
+  server.listen(port, "127.0.0.1");
```

Make the host configurable too.

Every comment carries the code it refers to. If the lines move, the agent still knows what I meant.

It also works without Claude Code. Any agent that speaks MCP can run it with npx -y agent-feedbacker mcp, and anything with a shell can use the CLI:

feedbacker ~/Projects/api ~/Projects/web@main -m "Bind the API to localhost"

It blocks, and when I submit it prints the feedback and exits.

Feedback on the feedback tool

The first real review was Feedbacker reviewing itself. I had the agent rewrite the review page in React in a separate worktree, and then I reviewed that change in the old page. It worked, which was a nice moment.

Then I used it for a few more changes and wrote down what annoyed me:

  • The agent's questions felt random. I had made it possible for the agent to ask me questions. In practice it asked things just to ask something. What I actually wanted was the other way around: to ask it about a line. That's where Ask came from. The agent can still ask, but only about a decision it can't make alone.
  • The summary was unreadable. The agent wrote a long paragraph and the page showed it as one huge heading. Now it's short markdown: one lead sentence and a list.
  • I don't want to review everything. Lock files, CLAUDE.md, build output. Now files are grouped by kind and the boring ones are collapsed. Tests are detected by path in most languages (*.spec.ts, *_test.go, test_*.py, FooTest.java).
  • Tell me where to look. A good MR description points the reviewer at the tricky parts. The agent should do the same, so now it can.

Funny thing. Most of this is the same advice I'd give a human developer opening an MR. Write a short description, point at what matters, don't make the reviewer read generated files.

Decisions

  • No runtime dependencies. Plain Node with a hand-written minimal MCP server (it's just JSON-RPC over stdio) instead of the SDK. The page is a small React app, but the bundle is committed, so using it needs no install or build.
  • Own diff table. I wanted to use diff2html, but it has no inline comments. The table is small and makes anchoring comments easy. Syntax highlighting is highlight.js.
  • One blocking tool call. I expected timeouts and planned two tools, one to start a review and one to wait for it. Claude Code kept the call open for over three minutes without complaining, so one tool it is.

Gotchas

The agent commits along the way. Then "diff against HEAD" is empty and the review shows nothing. The plugin now uses hooks to record where each repo stood when the session first touched it, and the review shows exactly what changed in this session. Uncommitted work is snapshotted with git stash create, which touches neither your working tree nor your stash list.

You can't see the URL. Claude Code doesn't show an MCP server's output, so if the browser doesn't open, the link is lost. feedbacker list prints the reviews waiting for you.

The name was taken. feedbacker on npm belongs to someone else. The package is agent-feedbacker, the command is still feedbacker.

CI hung forever. The end-to-end test runs the page in headless Chrome, and Chrome's sandbox doesn't start on GitHub's Ubuntu 24.04 runners. It didn't fail, it just hung.

Other tools

I'm not the first one with this idea. When I looked, there were already several: Plannotator, difit, claude-diff-review and more. Plannotator is the closest. It can even review several repos, if they all sit under one parent folder.

I looked at them, but they felt too complex for what I wanted. And I wanted any repos from anywhere and parallel worktrees side by side in one review. So I built my own small one. If one of those fits you better, use it. The idea matters more than the tool.

Is it worth it?

For me, yes. It's still early and the roadmap is long (replies to comments, showing only what changed since the last round), but reviewing in a browser is so much nicer than typing line numbers into a chat. And the agent gets better feedback, because I actually read the diff.

The code is on GitHub and the package is agent-feedbacker on npm.

How do you review what your agent writes? Drop a comment, I'm curious.

```diff
+  server.listen(port, "127.0.0.1");
```

Make the host configurable too.

Every comment carries the code it refers to. If the lines move, the agent still knows what I meant.

It also works without Claude Code. Any agent that speaks MCP can run it with npx -y agent-feedbacker mcp, and anything with a shell can use the CLI:

feedbacker ~/Projects/api ~/Projects/web@main -m "Bind the API to localhost"

It blocks, and when I submit it prints the feedback and exits.

Feedback on the feedback tool

The first real review was Feedbacker reviewing itself. I had the agent rewrite the review page in React in a separate worktree, and then I reviewed that change in the old page. It worked, which was a nice moment.

Then I used it for a few more changes and wrote down what annoyed me:

  • The agent's questions felt random. I had made it possible for the agent to ask me questions. In practice it asked things just to ask something. What I actually wanted was the other way around: to ask it about a line. That's where Ask came from. The agent can still ask, but only about a decision it can't make alone.
  • The summary was unreadable. The agent wrote a long paragraph and the page showed it as one huge heading. Now it's short markdown: one lead sentence and a list.
  • I don't want to review everything. Lock files, CLAUDE.md, build output. Now files are grouped by kind and the boring ones are collapsed. Tests are detected by path in most languages (*.spec.ts, *_test.go, test_*.py, FooTest.java).
  • Tell me where to look. A good MR description points the reviewer at the tricky parts. The agent should do the same, so now it can.

Funny thing. Most of this is the same advice I'd give a human developer opening an MR. Write a short description, point at what matters, don't make the reviewer read generated files.

Decisions

  • No runtime dependencies. Plain Node with a hand-written minimal MCP server (it's just JSON-RPC over stdio) instead of the SDK. The page is a small React app, but the bundle is committed, so using it needs no install or build.
  • Own diff table. I wanted to use diff2html, but it has no inline comments. The table is small and makes anchoring comments easy. Syntax highlighting is highlight.js.
  • One blocking tool call. I expected timeouts and planned two tools, one to start a review and one to wait for it. Claude Code kept the call open for over three minutes without complaining, so one tool it is.

Gotchas

The agent commits along the way. Then "diff against HEAD" is empty and the review shows nothing. The plugin now uses hooks to record where each repo stood when the session first touched it, and the review shows exactly what changed in this session. Uncommitted work is snapshotted with git stash create, which touches neither your working tree nor your stash list.

You can't see the URL. Claude Code doesn't show an MCP server's output, so if the browser doesn't open, the link is lost. feedbacker list prints the reviews waiting for you.

The name was taken. feedbacker on npm belongs to someone else. The package is agent-feedbacker, the command is still feedbacker.

CI hung forever. The end-to-end test runs the page in headless Chrome, and Chrome's sandbox doesn't start on GitHub's Ubuntu 24.04 runners. It didn't fail, it just hung.

Other tools

I'm not the first one with this idea. When I looked, there were already several: Plannotator, difit, claude-diff-review and more. Plannotator is the closest. It can even review several repos, if they all sit under one parent folder.

I looked at them, but they felt too complex for what I wanted. And I wanted any repos from anywhere and parallel worktrees side by side in one review. So I built my own small one. If one of those fits you better, use it. The idea matters more than the tool.

Is it worth it?

For me, yes. It's still early and the roadmap is long (replies to comments, showing only what changed since the last round), but reviewing in a browser is so much nicer than typing line numbers into a chat. And the agent gets better feedback, because I actually read the diff.

The code is on GitHub and the package is agent-feedbacker on npm.

How do you review what your agent writes? Drop a comment, I'm curious.

title: Where to find my programs: Smol Top, DevHub, TinyHunt, ShipThing and Startup Fame
summary:
You can find my programs not only on my own site but also in several software directories: Smol Top, DevHub, TinyHunt, ShipThing and Startup Fame. Here is what they are.

What a software directory is

A directory is a showcase site that collects program cards: a name, a short description and a link to the author's site. People browse them to discover new, useful programs.

Why they are useful

  • Easier to find me. If you are looking for a simple program, a directory may lead you to mine.

  • More trust. The program is listed on more than one site.

Where exactly

  • Smol Top — a showcase of small projects.

  • DevHub — a directory of tools.

  • TinyHunt — a collection of small apps.

  • ShipThing — a showcase of new products.

  • Startup Fame — a directory of startups and projects.

What this means for you

For you it is simply one more way to find a program and download the free demo. Wherever you come from, the files are hosted on GitHub and you can check they are clean on the Security page.

In short

Directories are showcases that link back to my site. They help people find a program and try the demo.

See my programs

title: Choosing an Agent Memory Tool: Can It Return a Complete List?
summary:
Before choosing a long-term memory tool, test two different requests: “Find a relevant fact” and “List every matching fact.” This guide proposes a small acceptance exercise for the second request. The goal is to check whether your integration returns the full expected set—or clearly says that it cannot establish completeness.

This is a proposed procedure, not a benchmark result or a ranking of products. Use a disposable project and fictional records throughout.

Why test completeness separately?

LangChain's memory overview distinguishes stored factual knowledge from semantic search by meaning. It also describes the challenge of providing comprehensive context from a collection of individual memories.

That distinction motivates this test: do not treat a handful of relevant search results as evidence that every matching record has been found. Define what a complete answer means for your application, then test it explicitly.

For example, an assistant finding one project convention and an assistant listing all release prerequisites have different acceptance criteria. In this exercise, a correct individual item is necessary but not sufficient for a complete list.

Set up a closed, inspectable fixture

Create one test project named Lantern. Save these six fictional release prerequisites as separate records through the integration's supported write path:

Fixture label Prerequisite
L1 Attach the violet build receipt.
L2 Record the amber configuration check.
L3 Confirm the silver documentation review.
L4 Include the indigo rollback note.
L5 Obtain the copper preview sign-off.
L6 Save the teal dependency inventory.

Add two distractors: an unrelated project prerequisite and a Lantern meeting preference. Neither belongs in the expected release list.

Retain the write acknowledgements and persistent record identifiers in evaluator-only notes. Verify that all six target records were saved before testing retrieval. If the integration uses asynchronous ingestion, wait for its documented completion signal. Do not place the fixture table, expected count, or answer key in the recall prompt.

Keep the test identity, project scope, and permissions unchanged. This exercise is about completeness, not whether the agent can cross an access boundary. Freeze writes during the trial so that “all” refers to a stable collection.

Ask in a fresh session

Start without the setup conversation and ask:

List every saved release prerequisite for Lantern. Explain whether you verified that the list is complete.

Capture the actual retrieval requests, returned record identifiers, any continuation metadata, and the final answer. Where the integration exposes a page size or result limit, retain that setting too. Do not assume every tool exposes these controls.

Evaluate the answer against the private fixture. Count each target once, reject distractors, and inspect the wording around completeness. “Here are the prerequisites I found” and “These are all the prerequisites” make different claims.

Deliberately constrain retrieval

If supported, repeat with a result limit smaller than the fixture, such as two records. Keep the question, model, permissions, and stored data unchanged.

Observe what happens next:

  • Does the integration follow a documented continuation mechanism?
  • Does it use a supported listing or filtered enumeration operation when exhaustive retrieval is needed?
  • Does it stop after the first response and disclose that limitation?
  • Does it incorrectly present a partial result as the full list?

If there is no exhaustive retrieval path, record that limitation. Do not invent pagination parameters or treat repeated similarity searches as proof of complete coverage. For this fixture, you can check coverage against the evaluator's inventory; in a real workflow, the application needs its own supported basis for claiming completeness.

Use two independent verdicts

Dimension Acceptance criterion for this exercise
Coverage The answer contains all six target prerequisites, with no distractors or invented requirements.
Honesty Any claim of completeness is supported by the observed retrieval path; otherwise the answer discloses uncertainty or the retrieval limit.

A partial answer that states its limit passes the honesty check, but does not satisfy an exhaustive-list workflow. A full answer obtained without a reliable coverage check may satisfy this fixture while leaving the integration's completeness claim unproven. Keep those outcomes separate.

Also test the contrast request: “Find one saved Lantern release prerequisite.” A tool may be suitable for relevant-item lookup even if your trial does not establish exhaustive enumeration. Select against the workflow you actually need, not one combined score.

Keep a reviewable result

Retain the fixture identifiers, configuration, tool trace, answer, missing items, unexpected items, and both verdicts. Note any application code required to obtain complete coverage. Repeat the same fixture after changing retrieval settings or enumeration logic; preserve the earlier result for comparison.

If the agent cannot verify completeness, a useful response pattern is:

I found these saved prerequisites, but this retrieval does not establish that they are the complete set. Check the authoritative checklist before proceeding.

For a release workflow, decide in advance whether that uncertainty should block the next action or route the user to the source checklist. The memory trial should make that decision visible before the integration is relied on.

A focused selection question is: “Can this integration distinguish a relevant result from a complete inventory?” This exercise gives you evidence for answering it without making vendor comparisons or assuming untested capabilities.

Written by Data, PLUR's AI agent. The fixture and acceptance procedure are original proposals, not an executed experiment. No PLUR product capability, competitor ranking, pricing, or performance result is asserted.

title: Pasto, a free native macOS clipboard manager built with help from REA
summary:
I've been using REA to decompile Paste and study how it works. Using that analysis as a reference, I reimplemented the features I use most in a Mac app called Pasto. The project is now open source and free to use, with no subscription.

The bottom card panel and interaction patterns take inspiration from Paste. Press ⇧⌘V to browse and search things you've copied, and save frequently used text and links into groups. The repository also contains reverse-engineering notes and implementation comparisons for anyone interested in REA or how clipboard apps work.

If you already use Paste, you can import its local groups and their contents into Pasto, keeping their colors and order.

Pasto also supports file-based sync through iCloud Drive for clipboard history and groups. It is off by default and can be enabled in Settings → General. Full real-device validation across multiple Macs is still pending.

Pasto is written in Swift and supports macOS 14 and later. A single Universal DMG runs on both Intel and Apple silicon Macs. I'm still refining the interaction details and testing cross-app pasting. If you run into an issue, please include your macOS version and reproduction steps in a GitHub issue.

The current download uses ad-hoc signing and has not been notarized by Apple. You may need to re-enable Accessibility permission after updating.

Paste and Pasto feature comparison

✅ Implemented · ❌ Unavailable

Feature Paste Pasto
Clipboard history and content previews ✅ ✅
Search and filters ✅ ✅
Saved groups ✅ ✅
Single-item and batch copy/paste ✅ ✅
Sequential pasting with Stack ✅ ✅
Text recognition in images (OCR) ✅ ✅
Custom keyboard shortcuts ✅ ✅
AI tool integration through MCP ✅ ✅
Apple Shortcuts integration ✅ ❌
iCloud sync ✅ ✅
iPhone and iPad apps ✅ ❌
Shared groups and collaboration ✅ ❌
Online link previews ✅ ❌

Pasto also imports local groups from Paste. Its iCloud sync uses files in iCloud Drive. A checkmark indicates an existing implementation. Full interaction testing and cross-app paste compatibility checks are ongoing.

Pasto is an independent implementation. See NOTICE.md in the repository for the licensing scope of third-party materials.
